stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "p = 0.497", Sentence = "This model provided an excellent account of the covariance matrix reported by Fan et al. info.title: Questionable mediated effect of selfmanagement on athletic performance: A comment on Fan et al. (2026)

author.affiliation:
Department of Clinical Neuroscience
								
									Karolinska Institutet
									Stockholm
									Sweden

text.text: Drawing on the covariance matrix reported by Fan et al., I reassessed the empirical basis of their mediation model linking self-management to athletic performance.

I demonstrate that the observed covariance structure can be reproduced by a theoretically different latent-variable model that does not rely on the directional mechanism proposed in the original article.

In this alternative account, self-reported self-management, psychological resilience, competitive spirit, and athletic performance are conceptualized as indicators of a broader construct, core self-evaluation.
The results illustrate a broader inferential problem in psychological research: multiple theoretically plausible models may provide equally adequate explanations of the same correlational pattern.
Consequently, observational associations alone offer limited grounds for preferring one explanation over competing alternatives.
Researchers should therefore routinely evaluate alternative models when drawing inferences about psychological mechanisms from nonexperimental data.
The study by Fan et al. Fan et al. (2026) examined data from 772 Chinese track and field athletes of which 12% were female.
text.formatted: The study by <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Fan et al. Fan et al. (2026)</ref> examined data from 772 Chinese track and field athletes of which 12% were female.

text.text: Measures of self-rated self-management, psychological resilience, competitive spirit, and athletic performance were administered.
Based on a serial mediation analysis, Fan et al. concluded that "self-management is an important factor influencing the athletic performance of Chinese track and field athletes.

Its effect is reflected not only in its direct promotion of athletic performance but also in its indirect effect through the sequential psychological mechanism of psychological resilience and competitive spirit" (p. 1).
Fan et al.'s interpretation is one possible explanation of the observed data, but it is not the only one.
Correlational evidence generally cannot establish the causal ordering of psychological variables (Reichenbach, 1971).
text.formatted: Correlational evidence generally cannot establish the causal ordering of psychological variables <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Reichenbach, 1971)</ref>.

text.text: Distinct causal models may generate identical covariance structures, preventing researchers from determining which explanation is correct based solely on observed associations.
Consequently, conclusions regarding mechanisms may be influenced as much by theoretical assumptions embedded within statistical models as by the empirical observations themselves.

The purpose of this commentary is to illustrate this point through the presentation of an alternative model that reproduces the reported relationships while leading to a different theoretical interpretation.
All analyses were performed in R 4.5.3 (R Core Team, 2026) using the lavaan package (Rosseel, 2012).
text.formatted: All analyses were performed in R 4.5.3 (R Core Team, 2026) using the lavaan package <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Rosseel, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: The covariance matrix reconstructed from the summary statistics reported by Fan et al., together with the analysis code, is available on GitHub at https://github.com/KimmoSorjonen/26.08.M.
text.formatted: The covariance matrix reconstructed from the summary statistics reported by Fan et al., together with the analysis code, is available on GitHub at <ref type="url" target="https://github.com/KimmoSorjonen/26.08.M">https://github.com/KimmoSorjonen/26.08.M</ref>.

text.text: The proposed alternative model is displayed in Figure 1.
text.formatted: The proposed alternative model is displayed in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>.

text.text: Instead of treating self-management as the initiating variable in a causal chain ending in athletic performance, the model specifies self-rated selfmanagement, psychological resilience, competitive spirit, and athletic performance as indicators of a common latent construct, core self-evaluation.
Core self-evaluation reflects a person's overall appraisal of their own competence, worth, and effectiveness (Judge et al., 2004; Extremera and Rey, 2018).
text.formatted: Core self-evaluation reflects a person's overall appraisal of their own competence, worth, and effectiveness <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Judge et al., 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Extremera and Rey, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Under this framework, individuals with more positive core self-evaluations would be expected to report higher levels of self-management, psychological resilience, competitive spirit, and athletic performance.
This model provided an excellent account of the covariance matrix reported by Fan et al. (χ² = 1.40, DF = 2, p = 0.497, CFI = 1.000, TLI = 1.002, RMSEA = 0.000 [90% CI: 0.000; 0.064], SRMR = 0.007).
The theoretical implications of this model differ substantially from those suggested in the original article.
Fan et al. interpreted their results as evidence that self-management contributes to athletic performance through the intermediary roles of psychological resilience and competitive spirit.
By contrast, the latent-variable model treats all four observed variables as manifestations of an . . . . 1 underlying disposition.
Because both models reproduce the same covariance structure, the mediation effects highlighted by Fan et al. cannot be regarded as uniquely supported by the data.
Rather, they may reflect choices made during model specification rather than conclusions compelled by the empirical evidence.
The present reanalysis shows that the associations reported by Fan et al. can be accommodated by more than one theoretically coherent explanation.

Whereas the original article emphasized a sequential process in which selfmanagement influences athletic performance through psychological resilience and competitive spirit, the alternative latent-variable model explains the same pattern of correlations without assigning a causal precedence to self-management.
The aim of this commentary is not to argue that the original model is necessarily wrong.
Likewise, the good fit of the alternative model does not establish its correctness.
Rather, the key observation is that competing theoretical perspectives may account for the same set of empirical relationships.
When this occurs, statistical fit alone cannot identify the model that most accurately reflects the underlying psychological processes.
This limitation is particularly relevant for mediation analyses based on observational data.
Indirect effects are often interpreted as evidence of specific underlying mechanisms, yet cross-sectional and nonexperimental designs provide only limited information regarding causal direction.

When distinct models with contrasting theoretical implications fit the data well, conclusions regarding mechanisms, intervention priorities, and influencing pathways inevitably rest on assumptions that have not been directly tested.
For this reason, mediation results derived from observational datasets should be interpreted as tentative and conditional rather than as conclusive evidence of particular influencing processes.
This commentary is the latest in a series of critical evaluations of mediation analyses published in Frontiers in Psychology.
These commentaries have been submitted to Frontiers but have so far never been accepted for publication or even sent to review (Table 1).
